title: Sub-Vacuum Jamming for Secure Communication
authors: S. Barzanjeh, A. Poostindouz, B. C. Sanders
abstract: Artificial-noise jamming improves physical-layer security by degrading an eavesdropper's channel, but the injected noise also interferes with the legitimate receiver. We introduce a correlated-jamming protocol based on classical and quantum correlations that suppresses this self-interference while preserving the jamming penalty experienced by the eavesdropper. Bob broadcasts one mode of a correlated two-mode source and retains the second as a local reference. Eve, who has no access to the retained mode, receives the full thermal jamming field, whereas Bob uses an optimized joint measurement to cancel its correlated fluctuations. The residual self-jamming noise is governed by the conditional variance of the transmitted jamming quadrature given the retained reference. Any classically correlated source is bounded by the vacuum-noise floor and therefore restores Bob, at best, to his unjammed receiver noise. An entangled two-mode squeezed source surpasses this limit and produces sub-vacuum residual noise, with the maximum quantum advantage set by the transmissivity of the jamming path back to Bob. In the bright-source regime, this advantage becomes a fixed reduction in Bob's noise floor, independent of the signal and jamming powers. Within a bounded-collection wiretap model, correlated jamming preserves positive secrecy even when Eve has a stronger direct channel than Bob and remains effective against collective measurements on Eve's Gaussian output states. The protocol supports bright classical message transmission and requires no end-to-end quantum channel. Possible applications include shot-noise-limited optical communication, cryogenic microwave networks, and covert or power-constrained secure links.
summary: This paper introduces a correlated-jamming protocol to enhance physical-layer security in communication channels. By utilizing entangled two-mode squeezed vacuum sources, the legitimate receiver can actively suppress self-interference noise below the standard quantum limit. This method preserves positive secrecy even against powerful eavesdroppers and is applicable to various real-world systems like optical or microwave links.
main_problem: The goal is to improve physical-layer security in quantum communication by introducing correlated jamming noise that degrades an eavesdropper's channel while minimizing self-interference at the legitimate receiver.
main_result: Using entangled two-mode squeezed vacuum (TMSV) sources allows for sub-vacuum residual noise suppression, providing a measurable quantum advantage over classical jamming methods. This protocol maintains positive secrecy even when the eavesdropper has a stronger direct channel than the legitimate user.
method: The analysis uses an optimized joint measurement technique on the received field and a retained local reference mode to cancel correlated fluctuations induced by the jamming source.
model_or_system: The system models secure communication over lossy channels using a correlated-jamming protocol. It involves a bright coherent signal, a correlated two-mode source (classical or TMSV), and subsequent interference measurements at Bob's receiver.
key_observables: Self-interference noise variance ($\sigma_{B,J}$), achievable secrecy rate ($C$), and the quantum advantage quantified by residual noise below the vacuum floor.
important_parameters: Transmissivities of the channels ($\eta_{ch}, \eta_I$), signal power ($N_A$), and the squeezing parameter (for TMSV).
main_assumptions: The analysis is explicitly treated as a collective-attack bound, not a coherent-attack bound. It assumes specific channel loss models and idler storage efficiencies.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the setup: Alice sends signal $a_A$; Bob generates correlated source ($a_S, a_I$); $a_S$ is broadcast as jamming field $a_J$, and $a_I$ is retained for interference cancellation.
paper_structure: The paper develops the protocol by first defining the physical setup (correlated jamming), then deriving the noise suppression mechanisms using quantum optics, followed by quantitative comparisons of secrecy rates across different source types (classical vs. entangled) and attack models.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses practical limitations in quantum key distribution security by engineering active countermeasures (jamming) that leverage entanglement to surpass classical noise limits, which is highly relevant for physical implementations using superconducting circuits or optical links.
